subtopic_detail: Six weeks of morning abdominal pain with school non attendance in a thirteen year old who is well on weekends
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a thirteen year old girl who has attended school four days in the last six weeks. Each school morning she has stomach pain and nausea from about seven o'clock and cries when her mother insists she gets in the car.

On weekends and during the recent school holidays she was symptom free and went to a sleepover without difficulty. Her mother works from home and has been letting her stay in her room on the laptop. She has no truancy history, wants to keep up with her friends and says she feels sick at the thought of walking through the school gate.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender with no organomegaly or masses, growth tracking along the 50th centile with no weight loss, no pallor, no mouth ulcers, no joint swelling, mood reactive with normal affect during the consultation, no thoughts of self harm on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, faecal calprotectin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Certify her as medically unfit for school for four weeks and arrange educational materials to be sent home
options.rationale: Formalising absence removes the anxiety in the short term and reinforces avoidance, making return progressively harder as the time away lengthens. Medical certification for anxiety based non attendance is one of the commonest iatrogenic contributors to entrenched school refusal. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Refer her for an abdominal ultrasound and gastroenterology review before addressing the school attendance pattern
options.rationale: Her symptoms occur only on school mornings and resolve entirely at weekends and in school holidays, and her inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and calprotectin are unremarkable, so further gastrointestinal investigation is very unlikely to yield a diagnosis. Continued investigation also communicates to the family that a physical cause is still being sought. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on functional abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on functional abdominal pain

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her attendance and side effects in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is added when anxiety is severe or when a graded return program has not succeeded, and it does not by itself restore attendance. Beginning with medication also risks leaving the avoidance cycle and the school arrangements untouched. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Recommend enrolment in distance education so that she can continue learning without the distress of attending
options.rationale: Distance education removes the exposure that treatment depends on and isolates her from the peer contact she values, and it is considered only after an adequate graded return has failed or where there is a specific safety issue such as bullying. Choosing it now forecloses the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Arrange a graded return to school plan with the school wellbeing team and cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Anxiety based school refusal is treated with early graded exposure that returns the young person to school in planned steps, coordinated with the school so that arrival, a safe place and a staff contact are organised, alongside cognitive behavioural therapy for the anxiety. The longer the absence continues the harder return becomes, so this is arranged promptly rather than after further investigation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

explanation.summary: School refusal is anxiety driven non attendance in a young person who wants to succeed at school, and it is distinguished from truancy, in which the young person conceals the absence and shows no distress, and from withdrawal driven by depression, bullying or an undiagnosed learning disorder. The diagnostic signature is somatic symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea or headache that occur on school mornings and resolve on weekends and holidays, with a normal examination and unremarkable screening investigations. Management is prompt and collaborative: a graded return plan negotiated with the school, cognitive behavioural therapy for the young person, and coaching for parents on maintaining expectation of attendance while validating distress. Duration of absence is the strongest predictor of difficulty in returning, which is why certification of unfitness and early transfer to distance education are avoided. Screening for coexisting anxiety and mood disorders, bullying, learning difficulties and family stressors is part of assessment, and medication is added for severe anxiety or when a well delivered return program stalls.
key_points: Symptoms confined to school mornings with complete resolution on weekends and holidays is the defining pattern.
School refusal differs from truancy in that the young person is distressed and the parents know where they are.
Prompt graded return coordinated with the school plus cognitive behavioural therapy is first line.
Certifying unfitness or moving to distance education reinforces avoidance and worsens prognosis.
Screen for bullying, learning difficulty, depression and family factors as maintaining contributors.
explanation.pearls: The length of time out of school is the single best predictor of the difficulty of return, so a young person missing school for six weeks needs a return plan started within days rather than after a further round of investigations.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on functional abdominal pain

subtopic_detail: Excessive water drinking with a large diurnal weight gain and a falling sodium in a man with chronic schizophrenia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on the rehabilitation unit reviewing a 41 year old man with schizophrenia of twenty years duration who has been drinking from bathroom taps and carrying a two litre bottle everywhere.

Staff report he is more confused in the late afternoon than in the morning and vomited twice yesterday evening. He has been on the same dose of olanzapine for three years, takes no diuretic, and his fluid intake yesterday was documented as more than eight litres. His weight was 78.4 kg at seven in the morning and 82.1 kg at four in the afternoon.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mildly disorientated to time in the afternoon with normal orientation in the morning, no focal neurological signs, no asterixis, mucous membranes moist, no oedema, no postural drop in blood pressure, chest clear, no tremor or rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), urea 2.1 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), creatinine 58 micromol/L (60 to 110), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 88 mmol/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Restrict his fluid intake with a supervised plan and monitor twice daily weights against a target weight
options.rationale: Dilute urine with a low urine osmolality and low urine sodium in the setting of documented excessive intake identifies primary polydipsia, in which the kidney is appropriately excreting free water and the problem is the volume consumed. Supervised fluid restriction with diurnal weight monitoring is the treatment, and weight is used because it tracks water load hour by hour while sodium lags behind. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Commence hypertonic 3 per cent sodium chloride by infusion with hourly sodium measurement in a monitored bed
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures, obtundation or respiratory compromise, and he has only mild afternoon disorientation. Actively raising the sodium in a patient who will correct rapidly once drinking stops risks overcorrection and osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Commence demeclocycline to induce a nephrogenic response and repeat his electrolytes in seventy two hours
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is used in chronic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion where water restriction alone fails, and it is inappropriate when the kidney is already maximally diluting the urine. His urine osmolality of 88 mmol per kilogram excludes inappropriate antidiuresis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Cease olanzapine and substitute an antipsychotic with a lower reported association with hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can contribute to inappropriate antidiuresis, but that produces concentrated urine rather than the maximally dilute urine seen here, and abruptly changing an agent that has maintained stability for three years risks relapse. Medication review is reasonable later if the drinking persists despite behavioural measures. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Give intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride at a moderate rate and recheck his serum sodium after six hours
options.rationale: Isotonic saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, and he has moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and a low urea, all indicating water excess rather than volume depletion. Giving saline to a water overloaded patient adds to the load the kidney must excrete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Primary polydipsia affects a substantial minority of people with long standing schizophrenia and can progress to water intoxication with hyponatraemia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis and death. The biochemical signature separates it from other causes of hyponatraemia: serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is maximally dilute at well under 100 mmol per kilogram, and urea is low, indicating that the kidney is handling a large water load appropriately, whereas the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion produces inappropriately concentrated urine with urine sodium above about 30 mmol per litre. Symptoms characteristically worsen through the day as water accumulates, which is why diurnal weight monitoring against a target weight is the practical monitoring tool on inpatient units. Management is behavioural, with supervised fluid restriction, restricted access to water sources, weight based escalation protocols and treatment of the underlying psychotic illness, and severe symptomatic hyponatraemia is managed with hypertonic saline in a monitored setting. Overcorrection is a real hazard in this group because the sodium can rise very quickly once drinking stops.
key_points: Maximally dilute urine with low urine sodium and low urea distinguishes primary polydipsia from inappropriate antidiuresis.
Symptoms worsen through the day as water accumulates, so afternoon confusion with morning clarity is characteristic.
Diurnal weight change against a target weight is the practical bedside monitor of water load.
Supervised fluid restriction is the treatment; hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or obtundation.
Sodium can rise rapidly once drinking stops, so overcorrection and osmotic demyelination are genuine risks.
explanation.pearls: A rise of more than about three to four per cent of body weight between morning and late afternoon is the practical threshold used on inpatient units to trigger fluid restriction and urgent electrolyte measurement, because it identifies dangerous water loading before the sodium has fallen far.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Longstanding sensory based food restriction with faltering growth in a thirteen year old with no body image concern
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a thirteen year old boy referred because he has dropped from the 50th to below the 10th centile for weight over two years. He eats six foods, all beige and dry, and gags at the smell of cooked vegetables.

His mother says he has eaten this way since he was three and that mealtimes have always been a battle. He says he would like to be bigger and stronger for football and has never tried to lose weight or felt fat. He has no vomiting, laxative use or exercise rituals, and his periods of restriction do not vary with his mood.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 52 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg sitting with no postural drop, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index on the 5th centile for age, no lanugo hair, no parotid swelling, no dental erosion, no callus on the knuckles, testicular volume and pubic hair at Tanner stage 3, no oedema, mood euthymic with normal affect
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, magnesium and phosphate within normal limits, ferritin 14 micrograms/L (30 to 200), zinc below the reference interval, coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, electrocardiogram showing sinus bradycardia at 52 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 410 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence family based treatment focused on parental control of eating to restore weight and challenge weight concerns
options.rationale: Family based treatment is the first line for anorexia nervosa in adolescents and its central task, externalising an illness that drives weight and shape concern, does not map onto restriction driven by sensory aversion. Elements of parental support for intake are used, but the treatment model and the exposure work differ. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Prescribe an appetite stimulant and arrange follow up of his weight in the general paediatric clinic in three months
options.rationale: Appetite is not the limiting factor when food is refused because of its smell, texture or appearance, and pharmacological appetite stimulation has little evidence in this disorder. Three months of monitoring without intervention would allow further growth faltering. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary team for dietetic nutritional rehabilitation with graded sensory exposure to new foods
options.rationale: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder driven by sensory sensitivity is treated by combining dietetic work to correct energy and micronutrient deficits with graded exposure that systematically introduces new foods, alongside parent coaching and screening for coexisting autism and anxiety. Weight restoration and exposure proceed together because nutritional repletion alone does not broaden the diet. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Admit him to a medical ward for nasogastric feeding and cardiac monitoring because of his resting bradycardia
options.rationale: Admission is driven by medical instability such as a heart rate under about 40 beats per minute, postural instability, hypothermia, electrolyte derangement or a prolonged corrected QT interval, none of which he has. Admitting a stable adolescent forfeits the outpatient exposure work that his disorder requires. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Arrange gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude an organic cause for his restricted intake and poor growth
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for dysphagia, odynophagia, vomiting, abdominal pain or positive coeliac serology, and his serology is negative with normal immunoglobulin A and his restriction is clearly sensory in character. Investigating further reinforces the search for a physical explanation and delays treatment. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on faltering growth)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on faltering growth

explanation.summary: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder is characterised by failure to meet nutritional or energy needs through avoidance driven by sensory characteristics of food, lack of interest in eating, or fear of an aversive consequence such as choking or vomiting, and it is defined by the absence of the weight and shape concerns that drive anorexia nervosa. It commonly begins in early childhood, persists for years before referral, and is strongly associated with autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and anxiety disorders. Consequences include growth faltering, micronutrient deficiencies such as iron, zinc and vitamins A, C and D, dependence on supplements, and marked psychosocial impairment around shared meals. Treatment is multidisciplinary, pairing dietetic rehabilitation with graded exposure to new foods and parent coaching, with cognitive behavioural approaches adapted for the fear based subtype and with medical admission reserved for genuine instability. Assessment includes measuring the micronutrients that a narrow diet predictably depletes, which are frequently abnormal even when the full blood count and electrolytes are normal.
key_points: Restriction is driven by sensory aversion, low interest or fear of aversive consequences, without weight or shape concern.
Coexisting autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and anxiety are common and shape treatment.
Micronutrient deficiencies such as iron and zinc occur even when routine bloods are normal.
Treatment combines dietetic nutritional rehabilitation with graded sensory exposure and parent coaching.
Admission is decided on medical instability, not on the diagnosis itself.
explanation.pearls: Asking directly whether the young person wants to be thinner is the fastest discriminator at the bedside: a boy who says he wants to gain weight to play football but gags at the texture of vegetables has sensory based avoidance, and treating him with an anorexia nervosa model wastes months.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on faltering growth
BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

subtopic_detail: Persistent dense amnesia with confabulation four weeks after treated Wernicke encephalopathy in a man who has stopped drinking
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar reviewing a 58 year old man on a rehabilitation ward four weeks after an admission with confusion, unsteadiness and abnormal eye movements, treated with parenteral thiamine.

His gait and eye signs have resolved and he has not drunk alcohol since admission. He cannot recall conversations from earlier the same day, and when asked what he did yesterday he describes in detail a fishing trip that the nurses confirm did not happen. He is alert, attentive to a digit span task and does not appear distressed, and he is due for discharge planning.

data_table.Examination: Alert with normal attention on digit span forwards and backwards, no nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia, gait steady without ataxia, dense anterograde amnesia with recall of no items at five minutes and no improvement with cueing, disorientation to date by three weeks, detailed confabulated accounts offered without hesitation, no tremor, no asterixis, mood euthymic with reactive affect
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count with mean cell volume 104 fL (80 to 100), liver function tests with gamma glutamyl transferase 180 U/L (less than 60), urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), computed tomography of the brain reported as generalised atrophy with no focal lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for his memory impairment and arrange review in the cognitive clinic in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors have no established benefit in alcohol related amnestic syndromes, in which the lesion is in the mammillary bodies and thalamic nuclei rather than in cholinergic projections. Their use here exposes him to adverse effects without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Continue oral thiamine and arrange formal neuropsychological assessment after several months of documented abstinence
options.rationale: Cognitive impairment after alcohol related brain injury continues to improve for months with sustained abstinence and nutritional repletion, so formal assessment is deferred until that trajectory has been allowed to run before any permanent conclusion about capacity or accommodation is reached. Ongoing thiamine is continued because deficiency frequently persists and further episodes cause additional damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine

options.text: Gently correct each confabulated account as it occurs so that he is repeatedly reoriented to what actually happened
options.rationale: Confabulation in this syndrome reflects a failure to retrieve and monitor memory rather than deliberate fabrication, and repeated confrontation produces distress without improving accuracy. Consistent orientation cues and a structured environment help more than correction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome

options.text: Apply for a guardianship order now so that permanent supported accommodation can be arranged before he is discharged
options.rationale: Substitute decision making may ultimately be required, but applying before the extent of recovery is known risks imposing a permanent arrangement on a man whose cognition may improve substantially over the coming months. Interim supported discharge with review is the proportionate step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine

options.text: Recommence high dose parenteral thiamine for a further three days and repeat cognitive testing at the end of that course
options.rationale: Parenteral thiamine is given for acute Wernicke encephalopathy and for high risk drinkers entering withdrawal, and he completed that treatment with resolution of his eye signs and ataxia. Repeating a parenteral course will not reverse established amnestic damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine

explanation.summary: Korsakoff syndrome is the chronic amnestic state that follows thiamine deficiency, classically after Wernicke encephalopathy, and is characterised by dense anterograde amnesia with variable retrograde loss, disorientation and confabulation, in the setting of preserved alertness, attention and immediate memory. The preservation of attention distinguishes it from delirium, and the isolated memory deficit with relatively intact other domains distinguishes it from a global dementia. Recovery is possible and often substantial: with sustained abstinence and nutritional repletion, cognition continues to improve over many months, so definitive statements about capacity, driving and long term accommodation are deferred rather than made at the point of medical stability. Management is continued thiamine, treatment of the alcohol use disorder, a structured environment with consistent routines and external memory aids, and formal neuropsychological assessment timed after a meaningful period of abstinence. Confabulation is best managed by orientation cues and redirection rather than confrontation, and families benefit from an explanation that the person is not lying.
key_points: Preserved attention with dense anterograde amnesia separates Korsakoff syndrome from delirium.
Confabulation reflects retrieval and monitoring failure, not deliberate deception, and confrontation is unhelpful.
Cognition improves for many months with abstinence and nutrition, so formal assessment is deferred.
Thiamine replacement continues because deficiency often persists and further episodes cause further damage.
Decisions about guardianship, driving and accommodation wait until the recovery trajectory is known.
explanation.pearls: Around a quarter of people with alcohol related brain injury recover substantially and a further half improve partially with sustained abstinence, which is why formal neuropsychological assessment is timed at several months rather than at the point of discharge.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome
